name_en: Xiping Old Tree Red Heart Tie Guan Yin
name_ru: Си Пин Хун Синь Те Гуань Инь
processing: Little is documented for this tea in particular. Traditional Anxi Tie Guan Yin is generally oxidised further than the modern green style, ball-rolled and then roasted.
harvest_season: Not documented for this tea; Anxi Tie Guan Yin is usually picked in spring and autumn, and those two pickings are the prized ones.
appearance_dry: Typically tight, dark green to brownish rolled pellets, as with traditionally made Anxi oolongs.
appearance_liquor: Typically golden to amber, deepening with the roast, as with traditional Tie Guan Yin.
appearance_wet: As with other Tie Guan Yin, thick whole leaves unroll from the pellets; red edges are usual in the more oxidised styles.
taste_profile: No reliable tasting record exists for this tea as such. Traditional Tie Guan Yin in general leans toward orchid, ripe fruit and gentle roast with a long sweet finish.

brewing.notes: The usual approach for rolled Anxi oolong: a quick rinse to open the pellets, water just off the boil, short early steeps.

vintage_note: Anxi Tie Guan Yin is normally sold by season and year, spring or autumn. Roasted traditional styles usually keep better than green ones and are often sold with some rest after roasting. Claims of tree age for this tea rest on the seller's word, so ask for the village, season and year.
description:
This name describes an Anxi Tie Guan Yin by three things: the place, Xiping; the plant, the red-heart type of Tieguanyin; and old trees. Xiping is the town usually named as the birthplace of Tie Guan Yin and of its making technique.

Growers distinguish red-heart and green-heart types of the plant. Little is documented about how this particular tea is made. A traditional Anxi lot would be more oxidised and roasted than the pale, vacuum-packed style that dominated for years, but that is a description of the wider class.

In the cup, expect the general traditional Tie Guan Yin direction: floral and fruity notes with some roast, and a sweet finish. Treat the first session as a test of this lot, because no independent tasting standard exists for the name.

Old tree is the weakest part of the label: no public standard defines it here. When buying, ask what the seller means by it and how they know. Compare it with a plain traditional Tie Guan Yin from the same seller before paying more.
history:
Xiping town in Anxi is widely named as the home of Tie Guan Yin, and the tea's discovery is commonly placed in the 1720s to 1730s. The split into red-heart and green-heart types is recorded in accounts of the plant.

Little is documented about old-tree red-heart Xiping tea as a named product. It appears mainly as a description used in the trade, not as a registered type.
